entries.name: Personal & Professional Development
entries.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

entries.name: Optimization Methods in AI
entries.text: Optimization Methods in AI studies search and optimisation for rational agents. Topics include uninformed and heuristic search, local and global optimisation, adversarial search, constraint satisfaction, linear programming and discrete optimisation. Laboratory exercises and projects develop algorithm implementation, evaluation and experimental investigation of small intelligent systems.

entries.text: Linear Algebra studies systems of equations, matrices, vectors, linear transformations and vector spaces. Students examine eigenvalues, orthogonality, least-squares approximation, quadratic forms and singular value decomposition. Applications include discrete signals, difference equations, Markov chains, dynamical systems, graphics and principal component analysis, with Mathematica supporting analytical problem-solving.

entries.name: Functional Anatomy
entries.text: Studies human anatomical structure in relation to function through regional and body-system blocks. Medical images, anatomical drawing, human-specimen material and guided practicals develop spatial reasoning, including observation in a dissection room. Historical, ethical and societal questions accompany these academic learning activities, which do not provide clinical qualification.

entries.name: Pharmacology
entries.text: Covers the science of drugs—their origin, composition, kinetics, therapeutic use and toxicity. Discusses drug targets, interactions and kinetics, enabling students to explain therapies in terms of molecular targets and physiological consequences.

entries.name: Infection & Immunity
entries.text: Explores fundamental processes in immunology such as recognition of self vs non‑self, lymphocyte receptor development and innate and adaptive immune responses. Examines host‑pathogen interactions, inflammation, tissue damage and immunopathology.

entries.name: Mechanisms of Disease
entries.text: Examines how normal organ-system function relates to disease. Students connect anatomy and physiology with symptoms, disease mechanisms, diagnosis, treatment and prognosis across digestive, cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, endocrine and nervous systems. Clinical cases and an imaginary-disease assignment develop coherent pathophysiological explanations.

entries.name: Neurobiology
entries.text: Neurobiology studies nervous systems and behaviour through comparative anatomy, evolution and physiology. Students examine animal behaviour, research models, welfare and research ethics, then connect biological rhythms and regulatory behaviour to sleep, lifestyle drugs, mood and eating disorders. Comparative-anatomy work and a literature-based report apply neurobiological concepts.

entries.name: Perception & Action
entries.text: Explores neural mechanisms behind perception and action. Examines how the brain processes sensory information and guides goal‑directed behaviour using methods from cognitive neuroscience and neuropsychology.

entries.name: Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine
entries.text: Introduces the molecular and cellular foundations of life and biomedical science. Topics include biological molecules, cells and membranes, communication, metabolism, cell division, heredity, gene expression and biotechnology. Students analyse scientific experiments and papers through teaching contributions and a research-based mini-symposium, with additional topics selected with the class.

entries.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
entries.text: Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.

entries.name: Molecular Cell Biology
entries.text: Provides foundation for practical applications in life science. Focuses on cellular biology of eukaryotes and prokaryotes, revisits concepts from introductory courses, examines current research and encourages evaluating reproducibility and modernising methods.

entries.name: Human Physiology
entries.text: Studies normal functioning of the human body, covering structure‑function relationships, energy handling, homeostasis, signalling, organ systems and integration of their functions.

entries.name: Biochemistry
entries.text: Explores the chemistry of life and biomolecules such as proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids. Discusses metabolic pathways, the role of biomolecules in health and disease and applications in medicine, biotechnology and sustainability.

entries.name: Life Science Laboratory
entries.text: Introduces biochemical and molecular laboratory work. Covers themes like blood, proteins, bacteria, DNA and bioinformatics and provides a foundation for clinical and biomedical research.

entries.name: Molecular Pathology & Genetics
entries.text: Covers general and molecular pathology and genetics. Studies cell injury, death, inflammation, immunity, tissue repair, regeneration, fibrosis and neoplasia, examines genetic mutations and diseases, and discusses genetic testing and ethical considerations.

entries.name: Statistics & Experimental Methods
entries.text: Develops experimental-design knowledge and practical statistical analysis for health and behavioural research. Students choose, fit, diagnose and interpret multivariable models for group comparisons, categorical outcomes and latent constructs. R, primarily through R Commander, supports practical exercises; data-analysis papers and a poster connect research questions to appropriate models, assumption checks and clear reporting.

entries.name: Advanced Research Methods & Statistics
entries.text: Advanced Research Methods & Statistics introduces systematic reviews and meta-analysis to synthesise results across studies. Students use R to conduct analyses, work with data structures and packages, estimate treatment effects and examine their consistency across studies. Presentations and active research tasks develop evidence-synthesis skills.
